result: XXX wild-type C. elegans oocytes preferentially eliminate the extra X chromosome between metaphase I and metaphase II. All metaphase I spindles had 7 chromosomes (6 bivalents + 1 univalent X), but 71% of metaphase II spindles had only 6 chromosomes, significantly different from the 50% expected from random segregation (p=0.004). FISH confirmed that the extra X was deposited in the first polar body with >50% frequency.
evaluation: Claims C22-C30 provide converging evidence from chromosome counts and FISH experiments showing non-random segregation of the extra X chromosome in XXX worms. The data include appropriate controls (diploid worms), statistical analysis, and direct visualization of X chromosomes at both meiotic stages. The conclusion that univalents are preferentially eliminated is well-supported by the quantitative data.

result: In him-8 mutants with two X univalents, both univalents are preferentially deposited into the first polar body. While 96% of metaphase I embryos had 7 chromosomes, only 5% of metaphase II embryos retained 7 chromosomes, with 40% having 5 chromosomes (both X's eliminated). FISH confirmed that 40% of embryos deposited both X univalents into the first polar body, compared to 25% expected from random segregation.
evaluation: Claims C34-C43 provide comprehensive evidence from both live and fixed imaging combined with FISH that demonstrates preferential elimination of X univalents in him-8. The data are statistically significant (p<0.0001), match previous genetic studies, and include appropriate quantification. The conclusion is well-supported by multiple independent observations.

result: Achiasmate autosomes (chromosome V in zim-2 mutants) are preferentially deposited into the first polar body, similar to X chromosomes. While 41% of metaphase I spindles had two V univalents, only 5% of metaphase II spindles retained both V's, compared to 10% expected from random segregation (p<0.0002).
evaluation: Claims C44-C49 extend the findings from X chromosomes to autosomes using the zim-2 mutant. The data include FISH confirmation and statistical analysis showing significant deviation from random segregation. However, the authors note potential undercounting issues at diakinesis vs metaphase I, which they address by showing that even with this caveat, the bias remains significant. The conclusion is supported despite this technical limitation.

result: Univalents biorient at metaphase I but have reduced AIR-2 kinase loading and increased REC-8 cohesin retention compared to bivalents. REC-8 orientation and KNL-2 localization indicate biorientation. AIR-2 levels on univalents were 2.3-fold lower than on bivalents and 1.7-fold lower than on metaphase II chromosomes, while REC-8 levels were 1.7-fold higher on univalents than between homologs of bivalents.
evaluation: Claims C50-C54 provide multiple lines of evidence (REC-8 staining, KNL-2 localization, AIR-2 quantification) that univalents biorient but have altered protein loading. The fluorescence intensity measurements are quantified with appropriate statistics (n=8-15 embryos, p-values reported). The inference that reduced AIR-2 and increased REC-8 may affect cohesion loss is reasonable given the known roles of these proteins.

result: Univalents lag during anaphase I in both him-8 (X univalents) and zim-2 (V univalents) mutants. 90% of him-8 embryos had lagging chromosomes at anaphase I compared to 2% in wild-type. FISH confirmed these were X univalents (13/14 cases). Lagging chromosomes moved as single units (98% of cases), indicating maintained sister chromatid cohesion. Similar results were obtained for chromosome V in zim-2 mutants.
evaluation: Claims C55-C67 provide extensive time-lapse imaging and FISH data demonstrating that univalents lag during anaphase I and maintain cohesion. The data include large sample sizes (n=119 him-8, n=52 wild-type), FISH confirmation of chromosome identity, and extension to autosomes. The observation that lagging is specific to anaphase I (only 10% at anaphase II) supports the conclusion that univalents cause lagging.

result: Lagging univalents show biased movement toward the cortex during anaphase I, with 65% moving cortically. This bias is partially dependent on the contractile ring for late-lagging chromosomes: NMY-2 depletion reduced cortical resolution of late-lagging univalents from 64% to 43% (p=0.02), but had no effect on early-resolving univalents (p=0.8).
evaluation: Claims C68-C73 demonstrate a cortical bias in univalent movement using time-lapse imaging (n=181 lagging chromosomes) and functional perturbation (NMY-2 RNAi). The separation into early and late-resolving categories is justified by the timing of contractile ring ingression. The statistical analysis is appropriate and the differential effect of NMY-2 depletion on late vs early resolution supports a role for the contractile ring in capturing late-lagging univalents.

result: Accelerating contractile ring ingression by mel-11 mutation increases the segregation bias in him-8 from 3:1 to 23:1 (nulloX:diploX ova), indicating that faster furrow ingression captures more lagging univalents in the polar body.
evaluation: Claims C74-C75 provide genetic evidence supporting the contractile ring capture mechanism. The mel-11 data (Table 1) show a dramatic sevenfold increase in segregation bias with appropriate sample sizes (n=374-1763 progeny). This result complements the NMY-2 depletion experiments and strengthens the conclusion that contractile ring dynamics influence univalent capture.

result: The position of contractile ring scission is influenced by lagging univalent position. When no univalents lag, scission occurs at 50% spindle length. When a univalent moves to the polar body, scission occurs at 40% spindle length (deeper). When a univalent moves into the embryo, scission occurs at 59% spindle length (shallower).
evaluation: Claims C76 and C78 provide quantitative measurements of scission position relative to lagging chromosome fate. The data suggest that lagging chromosomes influence where scission occurs, consistent with a model where the contractile ring must pass the lagging chromosome before scission. However, the sample sizes and statistical analysis are not explicitly provided for these measurements, which is a minor limitation.

result: The septin tube physically traps late-lagging univalents. In 5/10 cases where the septin ring reached the lagging univalent, the univalent was trapped in the septin tube and moved outward with it. In 3/10 cases, the ring passed the univalent before tube formation and the univalent joined the polar body. In 2/10 cases, the univalent escaped the tube into the embryo.
evaluation: Claims C79-C82 provide direct visualization of the septin tube capturing lagging chromosomes using time-lapse imaging. The small sample size (n=10) is a limitation, but the detailed observations of three distinct outcomes provide mechanistic insight. The conclusion that the septin tube traps univalents is supported by the direct observations, though additional experiments would strengthen this finding.

result: ANI-3 depletion reduces the efficiency of univalent capture. ani-3(RNAi) in him-8 significantly reduced XO male progeny from 37% to 27% (p<0.001), suggesting compromised septin tube integrity allows univalents to escape. However, ANI-3 depletion did not increase XXX progeny frequency, suggesting additional mechanisms contribute to trisomy correction.
evaluation: Claims C83-C86 provide genetic evidence supporting the septin tube capture mechanism with large sample sizes (n=1960-2123 progeny). The lack of effect on wild-type worms is an appropriate control. The observation that XXX progeny don't increase despite reduced male progeny is puzzling but the authors acknowledge this may reflect additional mechanisms. The conclusion about septin tube integrity is supported but incomplete.

result: Univalents are offset toward spindle poles before rotation, and this offset biases which pole rotates to the cortex. At late metaphase I (pre-rotation), 46% of embryos had both univalents offset toward the same pole. After rotation, 57% had one or both univalents closer to the cortical pole, with 0% having both closer to the interior pole. In 6/8 clear time-lapse sequences, the univalent-proximal pole rotated to the cortex. Lagging chromosomes preferentially resolved toward the pole they were already close to (80% of 30 embryos), inconsistent with differential pulling forces after rotation.
evaluation: Claims C87-C95 provide evidence for an early anaphase bias mechanism based on univalent position before rotation. The fixed embryo data show clear asymmetry after rotation (57% vs 0%), and the time-lapse data (6/8 cases) support the model that offset position influences rotation direction. The observation that chromosomes resolve toward their initial pole (80%) argues against a cortical pulling force model. The evidence supports the proposed mechanism, though the small sample size for time-lapse tracking (n=8) is a limitation.

result: Spindle rotation contributes to the segregation bias. The mei-2(ct98) him-8 double mutant, which fails spindle rotation, produced significantly fewer male progeny (21%) than him-8 alone (36%, p<0.0001), suggesting that spindle rotation is involved in the early anaphase segregation bias.
evaluation: Claims C91-C92 provide genetic evidence that spindle rotation affects segregation bias with appropriate sample sizes (n=925-1440 progeny). However, the authors acknowledge that mei-2(ct98) has other phenotypes besides rotation failure, making it difficult to conclusively attribute the effect to rotation. The result is consistent with the proposed model but not definitive proof. Additional experiments with more specific rotation mutants would be needed to confirm this mechanism.

result: Aneuploid sperm contribute modestly to reducing XXX progeny. Male pronuclei from him-8 mothers showed 90% haploX, 8% nulloX, and 2% diploX (n=52), significantly different from random segregation (50%, 25%, 25%; p<0.0001). The 10% nulloX sperm make a small contribution to reducing XXX self-progeny frequency.
evaluation: Claims C97-C100 provide FISH data on pronuclear stage embryos showing non-random X chromosome distribution in sperm. The data match previous genetic studies and are statistically significant. The conclusion that nulloX sperm contribute modestly to reducing XXX progeny is reasonable, though the sample size (n=52) is relatively small. This result helps explain why ani-3(RNAi) and mei-2 mutations don't increase XXX progeny despite reducing male progeny.

result: The manuscript establishes that asymmetric female meiosis can partially correct pre-existing trisomy in C. elegans. While random segregation would predict high frequencies of trisomic offspring, XXX C. elegans have far fewer trisomic offspring than expected. The extra X chromosome is preferentially eliminated during anaphase I through two mechanisms: univalents lag and move toward the cortex, and late-lagging univalents are captured by the ingressing polar body contractile ring.
evaluation: Claims C1-C7 represent the main conclusions of the manuscript, which are well-supported by the extensive experimental evidence in the grouped results above. The manuscript provides multiple independent lines of evidence (chromosome counts, FISH, time-lapse imaging, genetic perturbations) that converge on the conclusion that asymmetric meiosis corrects trisomy through preferential elimination of univalents. This is a major conceptual advance in understanding meiotic error correction.

result: The manuscript proposes a novel evolutionary advantage for asymmetric female meiosis: the ability to correct trisomy by preferentially depositing extra chromosomes into polar bodies. This adds to previously recognized advantages including maximizing egg volume, preventing sperm aster interference, and preserving polarity gradients.
evaluation: Claims C8-C15 establish the context and propose the novel hypothesis. The background on asymmetric meiosis (C8-C14) is well-established knowledge supported by appropriate citations. The novel hypothesis (C15) is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript. This represents a conceptual advance in understanding why asymmetric meiosis is conserved across animal phyla.

result: The manuscript establishes theoretical expectations for univalent segregation. Accurate chromosome segregation depends on chiasmata between homologs. When chiasmata fail to form, univalents may segregate randomly at anaphase I or II, which should result in equal frequencies of haplo and diplo ova (trisomy) or nullo and diplo ova (crossover failure).
evaluation: Claims C16-C21 establish the theoretical framework based on established knowledge of meiosis and Mendelian genetics. These predictions are well-supported by citations and provide the null hypothesis against which the experimental observations are compared. The theoretical framework is sound and appropriately applied.

result: Previous work established that him-8 mutants have two X univalents at diakinesis and produce a fivefold excess of nulloX over diploX ova, indicating non-random segregation. This provides the genetic foundation for using him-8 as a model to study univalent segregation.
evaluation: Claims C31-C33 accurately cite and interpret previous work (Phillips et al., 2005; Hodgkin et al., 1979) that established the him-8 phenotype. These claims provide essential background for the current study and justify the use of him-8 as a model system. The interpretation of the cited work appears accurate.

result: The manuscript discusses the potential relevance to other organisms. Trisomic human females and triploid oyster females produce more euploid offspring than expected from random segregation, suggesting similar mechanisms may operate. However, differences exist: human and oyster oocytes often form trivalents rather than separate bivalents and univalents, and mouse XO oocytes preferentially retain univalents rather than eliminate them. The efficiency of univalent elimination in C. elegans appears optimized to correct trisomy without reducing haploid egg production from crossover failures.
evaluation: Claims C101-C108 appropriately cite relevant literature on other organisms and discuss both similarities and differences. The authors are appropriately cautious about extrapolating to other species given the differences in chromosome pairing and segregation. The conclusion about evolutionary optimization (C108) is supported by the data showing no significant decrease in haploid eggs from crossover failures. This discussion appropriately contextualizes the findings.
